hook.line: Everyone in a café knows when a show was thrown together or made with love. *Salta a la vista* and *se nota* are how you say what is plain to see.
hook.es: Salta a la vista que no ensayaron.
hook.en: It's glaringly obvious they didn't rehearse.

examples.es: Salta a la vista que no ensayaron.
examples.en: It's glaringly obvious they didn't rehearse.

examples.es: Se nota que le puso cariño.
examples.en: You can tell she put her heart into it.

examples.es: Salta a la vista que el café necesita pintura.
examples.en: It's glaringly obvious the café needs paint.

examples.es: Se nota mucho que Vale cocina con ganas.
examples.en: You can really tell Vale cooks with enthusiasm.

examples.es: Salta a la vista que la obra costó muy poco.
examples.en: It's glaringly obvious the play cost very little.

rule:
*Salta a la vista que…* literally says "it jumps to the eye that…": something is so clear nobody needs proof.
*Se nota que…* is the everyday twin: "you can tell that…". Add *mucho* to push it: *Se nota mucho que…*.

After either one, use the ordinary verb (*ensayaron*, *cocina*). You are stating a fact you can see, so no subjunctive.
Link with plain *que*: never *de que*.
The fixed phrase is *a la vista*, not *en la vista*.
smallPrint: Teachers call *salta a la vista* an impersonal expression of evidence: no one in particular is doing the noticing.

readAndPick.es: Salta a la vista que no ensayaron.
options: It's glaringly obvious they didn't rehearse.
It's glaringly obvious we didn't rehearse.
It's glaringly obvious she doesn't rehearse.

readAndPick.es: Se nota que le puso cariño.
options: You can tell they put their hearts into it.
You can tell she put her heart into it.
She can tell you put your heart into it.
Can you tell he's nervous?
Are you nervous that it shows?
Can you tell I'm nervous?

readAndPick.es: Se nota mucho que Vale cocina con ganas.
options: You can really tell Vale cooks with enthusiasm.
You can just about tell Vale cooks with enthusiasm.
Vale can really tell we cook with enthusiasm.

readAndPick.es: Salta a la vista que el café necesita pintura.
options: It's glaringly obvious the café needed paint.
It's glaringly obvious the café needs paint.
It's glaringly obvious the cafés need paint.

readAndPick.es: Salta a la vista que la obra costó muy poco.
options: It's glaringly obvious the play will cost very little.
It's glaringly obvious the play costs a lot.
It's glaringly obvious the play cost very little.

options: You can't tell she's tired.
You can tell she's tired.
She can't tell you're tired.

options: You can tell they've just rehearsed.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Salta a la vista ___ no ensayaron.* (*que* or *de que*) It's glaringly obvious they didn't rehearse.
yourTurn.answer: Salta a la vista que no ensayaron.
yourTurn.why: Spanish links the two parts with plain *que*, as English does with "that".

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Se nota ___ le puso cariño.* (*que* or *lo que*) You can tell she put her heart into it.
yourTurn.answer: Se nota que le puso cariño.
yourTurn.why: After *se nota* comes *que* and then the thing you can tell.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: It's glaringly obvious the café needs paint.
yourTurn.answer: Salta a la vista que el café necesita pintura.
accept: Se nota que el café necesita pintura.
yourTurn.why: The verb after *que* is an ordinary present, because it is a plain fact.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: You can tell Vale put her heart into it.
yourTurn.answer: Se nota que Vale le puso cariño.
accept: Se nota que Vale puso cariño.
yourTurn.why: *Se nota que* works for anyone: just add who and what.

yourTurn.prompt: Say, a man speaking to a friend: Can you tell I'm nervous?
yourTurn.why: The question keeps the same frame, with *estoy* for how you feel.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Se nota que está cansada.* (You can tell she's tired.)
yourTurn.answer: No se nota que está cansada.
yourTurn.why: Put *no* in front of *se nota*: you can't tell.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it stronger: *Se nota que cocina con ganas.* (You can really tell she cooks with enthusiasm.)
yourTurn.answer: Se nota mucho que cocina con ganas.
yourTurn.why: *Mucho* goes right after *se nota* and turns the volume up.

pitfalls.wrong: Salta a la vista de que no ensayaron.
pitfalls.right: Salta a la vista que no ensayaron.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English "obvious that" has no extra word, and neither does Spanish: plain *que*.

pitfalls.wrong: Salta a la vista que no ensayaran.
pitfalls.right: Salta a la vista que no ensayaron.
pitfalls.why: Almost. It is a plain fact you can see, so the verb stays in the ordinary past, with no subjunctive.

pitfalls.wrong: Salta en la vista que no ensayaron.
pitfalls.right: Salta a la vista que no ensayaron.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The set phrase is *a la vista*, and it does not change.

personal: Think of something that shows when someone cares, or doesn't. Say it: *Se nota que…*.
